------------------------------------------------
EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  
Head Start and the Development of Life-Cycle Skills  
------------------------------------------------

=============================
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY
=============================
Preferred design: Within-family (sibling) fixed-effects, supplemented with an IV that uses county-year Head Start funding per poor 3- to 4-year-old.

Why this strategy?
• NLSY79 follows a nationally representative sample of mothers and *all* their biological children, so many families contribute ≥2 children with differing preschool experiences.  
• A sibling FE design wipes out all time-invariant family background factors (parental ability, preferences, neighbourhood, culture).  
• Remaining within-family variation in Head Start take-up is plausibly driven by idiosyncratic factors (program slot availability, birth-order timing relative to local funding expansions, mother’s varying employment status) that are plausibly exogenous after conditioning on observed time-varying covariates.  
• Adding an instrument based on *exogenous program supply* (log federal Head Start grants per poor preschool-age child in the county and year when the child was age 3–4) tightens identification by purging residual within-family selection (e.g., parents might send the child perceived to be “behind” to Head Start).

Formally  

(1) First stage:  
HS_ij = π Z_jt + θX_ij + λ_j + ε_ij         

(2) Second stage (main outcome Y):  
Y_ij = β ĤS_ij + θ′X_ij + λ_j + u_ij

where i = child, j = family, Z = county-year HS funding, λ_j = family FE, X = time-varying child controls.

=============================
2. TREATMENT & CONTROL
=============================
Treatment variable  
HS_ij = 1 if child i ever attended Head Start (reported in mother or child supplement) *before kindergarten entry*; 0 otherwise.

Control group  
Primary: biological siblings in the same family who did *not* attend any Head Start centre.  
Secondary (robustness): siblings who attended *other* preschool programs but not HS, to isolate HS-specific effects.

Timing / key variation  
Within a family, birth-order and cohort timing relative to local HS funding expansions generate quasi-random exposure. Treatment measured at ages 3–4, outcomes measured from middle-childhood (cognitive tests) through adulthood (education, employment, earnings).

=============================
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS
=============================
A1. Shared unobservables constant within family  
All stable family-level traits are differenced out by λ_j. Plausible because parents, permanent income, neighbourhood largely fixed across siblings.

A2. Exogeneity of *within-family* variation conditional on covariates  
After controlling for child sex, birth-order, age gaps, maternal age at birth, and pre-treatment health, the decision of which child attends HS is unrelated to potential outcomes. Reasonable given slot-constraint timing and program rationing, but addressed further with IV.

A3. Relevance and exogeneity of IV  
County-year HS funding strongly predicts participation (relevance); federal grant allocation rules depend on census-measured poverty counts, not on any individual child’s unobservable endowment (exogeneity). Mobility before age 3 is low, supporting exogeneity.

A4. SUTVA (no cross-child spillovers across families)  
Head Start participation of one child does not affect outcomes of non-siblings in the sample. Likely satisfied; intra-family spillovers matter but are absorbed by λ_j.

=============================
4. MAIN THREATS & MITIGATION
=============================
T1. **Sibling-specific selection**  
Parents may target the weaker child for HS.  
→ Include pre-treatment child endowments (birth weight, early health index) and use HS funding IV. Run placebo on those endowments to test for selection.

T2. **Program supply correlated with local shocks**  
HS funding increases may co-move with county economic cycles that also affect long-run outcomes.  
→ Add county-year controls (unemployment rate, median income) and state-year fixed effects; cluster SEs at county level.

T3. **Differential attrition / sample selection**  
Outcome data missing disproportionately for movers or disadvantaged children.  
→ Show balance tests on attrition; use IPW (inverse-probability weights) and Lee (2009) bounds as robustness.

=============================
5. R CODE OUTLINE
=============================

```r
# ---- 0. Packages ----
library(data.table)   # fast data manipulation
library(fixest)       # high-dim FE & IV
library(sandwich)     # robust vcov
library(lmtest)

# ---- 1. Load & Merge ----
# Assume three CSVs: child.csv, mother.csv, hs_funding.csv
child   <- fread("child.csv")      # child-level supplement
mother  <- fread("mother.csv")     # NLSY79 mothers
funding <- fread("hs_funding.csv") # county-year HS grants & demographics

dt <- merge(child, mother, by = "mother_id")
dt <- merge(dt, funding,
            by.x = c("county_code", "year_child_age3"),
            by.y = c("county_code", "year"),
            all.x = TRUE)

# ---- 2. Variable Construction ----
dt[, treat := as.integer(headstart == 1 & age_headstart <= 5)]

# Instrument: log funding per poor 3-4 y.o.
dt[, iv_fund := log(1 + hs_grant / poor_pop_3_4)]

# Family FE id (= biological mother)
dt[, fam_id := mother_id]

# Child-level controls
dt[, birth_order := frank(birth_year, ties.method="first"), by = fam_id]
controls <- c("male", "black", "hispanic",
              "birth_order", "bw_oz",          # birth weight
              "mother_age_birth", "mother_edu_pre")

# Outcome examples
dt[, lnhinc := log(1 + adult_income)]
dt[, hs_grad := as.integer(hs_grad == 1)]

# ---- 3. MAIN SPECIFICATION ----
# Example: log adult income
fmla1 <- as.formula(paste("lnhinc ~ treat | fam_id + county_year | 0 | county_code"))
mod1 <- feols(fmla1, data = dt, cluster = "county_code")

# IV with HS funding
fmla_iv <- as.formula(paste("lnhinc ~ 1 | fam_id + county_year | treat ~ iv_fund | county_code"))
mod2 <- feols(fmla_iv, data = dt, cluster = "county_code")

# Add controls
fmla_ivc <- as.formula(
  paste("lnhinc ~", paste(controls, collapse="+"),
        "| fam_id + county_year | treat ~ iv_fund | county_code"))
mod2c <- feols(fmla_ivc, data = dt, cluster = "county_code")

summary(mod2c)

# ---- 4. ROBUSTNESS CHECK: Placebo on Birth Weight ----
placebo <- feols(bw_oz ~ treat | fam_id + county_year, data = dt, cluster = "county_code")
summary(placebo)

# ---- 5. Save results ----
etable(list(OLS = mod1, IV = mod2c, Placebo = placebo),
       file = "headstart_results.tex")
```

=============================
6. EXPECTED RESULTS
=============================
Theory and prior evidence (human-capital accumulation, Deming 2009) suggest *positive* long-run effects:

• Cognitive / achievement test scores: ~0.15 σ increase at ages 8–14  
• High-school graduation: +5–7 percentage points  
• Log adult earnings: +0.05–0.10 (~5–10 %) by age 25–30  
• Employment probability: +3 p.p.  

Larger gains anticipated for boys and for the most disadvantaged families.

=============================
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST (Self-Assessment)
=============================
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = doubtful)

1. Strong first stage (IV relevance) ............... 1  
2. Exogeneity / no omitted within-family variables .. 0.8  
3. No differential measurement error ................ 0.9  
4. No spillovers / SUTVA across families ............ 1  
5. Attrition unbiased or corrected .................. 0.7  

Overall internal validity ≈ 0.88 (solid but not bullet-proof; main caveat is within-family selection and attrition).
